title: Chestnut and honey cake
subtitle: a dense, earthy loaf cake made with chestnut flour and set honey
excerpt: Chestnut and honey cake is a moist, dense loaf cake made with a mix of chestnut flour and plain flour. Chestnut flour gives the crumb a distinctively earthy, slightly sweet flavour and a heavier texture than a standard loaf cake. The honey keeps it moist and adds a floral sweetness that works well against the earthiness of the chestnut.
sourceNotes: Chestnut flour cakes documented in Italian and Corsican cooking from at least the medieval period, where chestnuts were a staple food in highland regions. The Tuscan castagnaccio is a related preparation; this recipe adds butter and honey for a lighter, more accessible result.

recipe.freezeNotes: Slice before freezing. Wrap individual slices and freeze for up to 2 months. Thaw at room temperature.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps at room temperature, wrapped, for 4 to 5 days. The flavour improves on the second day.

content.text: Chestnut and honey cake is a loaf cake built on chestnut flour, which gives the crumb an earthy, slightly sweet flavour unlike any other flour. The honey adds floral sweetness and keeps the crumb moist. A loaf cake in this style keeps well for several days and is better the day after baking.
Heat the oven to 170 degrees C (fan 150 degrees C / gas 3 to 4). Grease and line a 900 g loaf tin.
Beat the softened butter, honey, and caster sugar together until light and creamy, about 3 minutes. Beat in the eggs one at a time, then the vanilla extract.
Fold in the sifted chestnut flour, plain flour, and baking powder in two additions, alternating with the milk, until just combined. The batter will be slightly stiffer than a standard sponge.

Spoon into the prepared tin and smooth the top. Bake for 45 to 50 minutes until a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean. If the top is browning too quickly, cover loosely with foil after 30 minutes.
Leave to cool in the tin for 20 minutes, then turn out onto a rack.

attrs.problem: Cake very dense and heavy rather than moist
attrs.avoid: Avoid all chestnut flour with no plain flour addition; chestnut flour on its own produces a very dense, compact crumb.
attrs.fix: The 60:40 ratio of chestnut to plain flour in this recipe is the balance point. If you want a lighter result, shift to 50:50.

attrs.avoid: Avoid old or stale chestnut flour; it oxidises and turns bitter once the packet is opened.
attrs.fix: Buy chestnut flour in small quantities and use within 3 months of opening. Store in an airtight container in the fridge.
